summary: Offers suggestions on how IEEE 802.1X authenticators should use RADIUS. The material also appears as a non-normative appendix in the IEEE 802.1X specification and is published as an RFC for information. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3580 gives guidance for how an IEEE 802.1X network port should exchange RADIUS messages with an authentication server. It explains relevant attributes, accounting details, VLAN assignment, and security concerns.

questions: how to assign vlan with radius tunnel attributes
what is the rc4 eapol-key frame
subtitle: How an 802.1X switch or access point uses RADIUS for authentication and accounting.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.1X can use a RADIUS server for central authentication and accounting, but RADIUS attributes were originally described for other access settings.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains how an 802.1X Authenticator should use selected RADIUS accounting and authentication attributes, assign VLANs, and handle an RC4 EAPOL-Key frame.
tldr.outcome: The document is Informational and its text also appears in a non-normative IEEE 802.1X appendix. It is updated by RFC 7268, and it warns about weaknesses in the RC4 EAPOL-Key descriptor.

today: RFC 3580 is an Informational document updated by RFC 7268. Its text warns that the RC4 EAPOL-Key descriptor is likely to be deprecated and describes weaknesses in that method.

sections.title: Roles in 802.1X Authentication
sections.content:
IEEE 802.1X provides authenticated access to Ethernet, Token Ring, and 802.11 wireless networks. It does not require a backend authentication server, but an Authenticator may act as a RADIUS client when an operator wants centrally managed authentication, authorization, and accounting.

The Supplicant is the device being authenticated. The Authenticator is the network entity that requires authentication, such as a bridge or access point. The Authentication Server checks the Supplicant's credentials. RADIUS support is optional in 802.1X, so this guidance is informational.
sections.plainLanguage: A network port can ask a central server to check a device before granting access. This memo explains how the port and server exchange authentication and accounting information.

sections.title: Accounting for Sessions
sections.content:
Most RADIUS accounting attributes keep their usual meaning in 802.1X. Acct-Terminate-Cause records why a session ended, with mappings for events such as Supplicant logoff, lost physical connectivity, or failed reauthentication. A successful reauthentication does not itself end the session.

Acct-Multi-Session-Id can link related accounting sessions when a Supplicant roams between access points. The memo suggests forming it from the original access point's MAC address, the Supplicant's MAC address, and a 64-bit NTP timestamp, encoded as ASCII hexadecimal digits. Acct-Link-Count may record the number of aggregated ports.
sections.plainLanguage: Accounting records can say why access ended and link together records when a device roams. This helps the server treat related connections as part of the same session.

sections.title: Authentication Attributes
sections.content:
The memo describes how the Authenticator uses RADIUS attributes. For example, NAS-IP-Address identifies the bridge or access point, NAS-Port identifies a bridge port or an access point association ID, and Called-Station-Id and Calling-Station-Id carry the access point and Supplicant MAC addresses in uppercase hexadecimal with hyphens.

802.1X does not use PAP or CHAP, so User-Password, CHAP-Password, and CHAP-Challenge are not used by its RADIUS clients. Framed-MTU reflects the network medium; the RFC recommends that servers send EAP packets no larger than 1496 octets for 802.11 because some stations cannot handle larger MTUs. Message-Authenticator MUST protect packets in a RADIUS/EAP conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RADIUS field has a specific meaning for a network port. Some fields do not apply to 802.1X, while others identify the port, device, or EAP exchange.

sections.title: Assigning a VLAN
sections.content:
A RADIUS server can tell an Authenticator to place a port in a particular Virtual LAN (VLAN). The memo specifies Tunnel-Type as VLAN (13), Tunnel-Medium-Type as 802, and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID as the VLAN identifier encoded as a string. The VLAN identifier is 12 bits and ranges from 1 to 4094.

If only one VLAN is being specified, the Tag field SHOULD be zero. A VLAN assignment can, for example, let a wireless host remain on the same VLAN while moving within a campus network.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can include three RADIUS tunnel attributes to select a VLAN for the authenticated device. The VLAN number is carried as a string, and the tag is zero when no alternative tunnel is specified.

sections.title: Security and the EAPOL-Key Frame
sections.content:
RADIUS for 802.1X inherits threats such as packet forgery, dictionary attacks, replay, and key-management problems. Packets carrying EAP messages MUST use Message-Authenticator, and the Authenticator must base its access decision on Access-Accept or Access-Reject rather than conflicting EAP message contents. The memo recommends support for IPsec and a shared secret of at least 16 octets.

The RC4 EAPOL-Key descriptor is not acknowledged, so a lost frame can leave the Supplicant and Authenticator with different keying material. The RFC says the descriptor is likely to be deprecated and describes weaknesses in default-key-only implementations, reused key material, and RC4 encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS messages need integrity protection, and the Authenticator must use the server's accept or reject decision. The memo also warns that the described RC4 key-delivery method has known weaknesses.

references.text: Rigney, C., Willens, S., Rubens, A. and W. Simpson, "Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS)", RFC 2865, June 2000.
